title: Present simple: be, have got and routines
tagline: Facts, routines and habits — the tense for what is always or usually true.
exam: Reading Part 6 — a text about someone's daily life
Speaking Part 1 — questions about your daily routine
why: The present simple is the tense of everyday life: what you do, what you have and what is always true. It brings together three things you already know — be, have got and the third-person -s — into one system that A2 Key tests again and again, from reading texts about people's routines to your own Speaking Part 1 answers.

hook.text: Miss Vega gives the class a survey. "How often do you study English?" Nadia writes: "I study every day, but my brother only studies on Fridays." Liam adds: "I haven't got a brother — I've got two sisters!"
hook.ask: Find the -s endings on the verbs in the story. Why does study become studies for Nadia's brother but stay study for Nadia?

diagrams.title: The present simple system
diagrams.caption: Ordinary verbs add -s/-es/-ies for he/she/it. The helper does carries the question and the negative, so the main verb goes back to its base form.

diagrams.title: -s / -es / -ies for he, she, it
diagrams.caption: If you can't say the word easily with just + s, it probably needs -es or -ies.

diagrams.title: Adverbs of frequency: where do they go?

branches.label: at the start or end for emphasis
items: I go swimming once a week.

use.point: Routines and facts — I, you, we, they

examples.text: We go to school at half past seven.

examples.note: close + s, a fact about the shop

use.point: have got — for family, pets and possessions

examples.text: I don't watch TV in the morning.

examples.note: question and short answer with does

examples.text: I always do my homework, but I never forget my football boots.
examples.note: adverbs of frequency before the main verb

watch_out.why: he/she/it needs the -s/-es/-ies ending on the verb.
he/she/it uses doesn't, not don't, in the negative.
does already carries the -s — the main verb goes back to its base form.
age uses be in English, not have got.
the adverb of frequency goes before the main verb, but after be.
in a question, has/have moves to the front, before the person.

l1.why: Spanish doesn't mark the verb specially for ella; English adds -s/-es/-ies for he/she/it.
Age uses be in English, not have got.
In English, the frequency adverb goes before the main verb, not after.
In British English, questions about possession usually add got after has/have.

remember.trick: He, she, it — don't forget the S!
remember.tip: Every time the subject is he, she or it, listen for the s on the end of the verb — studies, watches, has.

dialogue.title: Lunchtime survey
dialogue.context: At lunch, Nadia is doing a class survey about daily routines. She asks Liam some questions.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Hi Liam! Do you study English every day?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Yes, I do. I always study for twenty minutes after dinner.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I haven't got a sister — I've got two brothers.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: One of them plays football, but the other one doesn't like sport at all.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: And what about you? Do you walk to school?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No, I don't. My mum drives me every morning.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Thanks, Liam! That's my survey finished.

items.why: she takes does in a question.
I takes 've got, not 's got or has got.
teach ends in ch, so it takes -es: teaches.
he takes doesn't in the negative.

items.sentence: I ___ do my homework before dinner.
items.why: the frequency adverb goes before the main verb.
your brothers is plural, so it takes have.
the shop (it) takes the -s ending: closes.

can_do: I can talk about routines and facts using be, have got and ordinary verbs.
I can spell and pronounce the -s/-es/-ies ending correctly for he/she/it.
I can make negatives and questions with don't/doesn't and use adverbs of frequency in the right place.
summary: Present simple = routines, facts and things that are always true: be, have got and ordinary verbs.
he/she/it adds -s/-es/-ies to the ordinary verb: plays, watches, studies.
Negative and question use don't/doesn't — and the main verb goes back to its base form.
Adverbs of frequency go before the main verb, but after be: I always study. I'm never late.
have got is common for possession: I've got, she's got, have they got…?
